schools.summary: Ellicott aligns the verse with 2 Kings 12:1-2, notes the omitted 'seventh year of Jehu,' and glosses the name Jehoash/Joash ('Iahu is a man,' or 'fire,' cf. Isa. 33:14).
Clarke reckons Joash was only one year old when secreted from Athaliah (2 Chron. 22:10) and lays out the whole arc of the reign in advance.
Gill glosses the age briefly and defers to the parallel in Kings.
Henry frames the reign as a lesson for the young — happy to be under wise counsel like Joash under Jehoiada — and the rule to repeat men's good and name their evil sparingly.

Ellicott reads 'all the days of Jehoiada' against Kings' 'all his days while Jehoiada instructed him' — the king's rightness bounded by his tutor's life; Keil points to the temple-repair record of 2 Kings 12:5-17 and the restored Jahve-worship.
Henry warns that men may keep an external religion by education alone, the form outstripping the power — easier to build temples than to be temples to God.
Gill fixes 'for him' as the king (not the aged priest), and names one wife Jehoaddan, mother of Amaziah (2 Chron. 25:1).
Ellicott notes the verse is peculiar to the chronicler's source, where Kings (2 Kings 12:3) instead has the un-removed high places.
Henry draws a counsel of prudence: young people should take advice in marriage, as Joash left the choice to Jehoiada, remembering the plagues of Jezebel and Athaliah.
Gill dates the resolve to about the king's twentieth or twenty-first year, after his marriage.
Clarke: the temple had been pillaged for Baal and left to decay under Joram and Athaliah (cf. v.7).
Ellicott renders 'was minded' as 'it became with the heart of Joash' (2 Chron. 6:8; 1 Kings 8:18), 'to repair' as 'restore,' and notes the chronicler paraphrases Kings and adds the Levites.
Henry commends church-repair as a good work needing active men, yet warns it is easier to build temples than to be temples to God.

themes: a purpose formed in the heart
a good work and its warning

schools.summary: Clarke: the temple being the whole nation's property, this is the first general collection for a house of God; 'from year to year' shows the extent of the decay.

Keil lays out the charge and the Levites' failure to hasten; Ellicott reads the command as the chronicler's version of Kings' 'each from his acquaintance,' the delay agreeing with 2 Kings 12:6 (unrepaired in the 23rd year).
Gill: the king called the priests and Levites to give them their charge.
Gill takes 'the chief' as the high priest and prime minister of state.

Wesley notes he is called only 'the chief' (perhaps by royal kinship or as head of a priestly family); Clarke identifies 'the collection of Moses' with the half-shekel poll-tax of Exod. 30:12-14, a ransom against plague.
Ellicott takes 'the tax of Moses' as a general designation, not the poll-tax, renders 'tent of the testimony' (Num. 9:15), and gives the differing form of the king's question in Kings.
Henry: the king outruns the priest in zeal, reproving Jehoiada's remissness — easier to build temples than to be temples to God.

debates.question: What is 'the collection of Moses' the Levites failed to bring in?

sides.position: The half-shekel poll-tax of Exod. 30:12-14, a ransom for souls
A general designation of the sanctuary moneys, not the poll-tax

schools.summary: Gill (with Kimchi): the 'sons of Athaliah' were her sons by another man, distinct from Ahaziah and his brethren.
Wesley: they were Ahaziah and his brethren (2 Chron. 21:17), acting at their mother's instigation; 'broke up' = broke open the treasuries and defaced the house.
Ellicott: Ahaziah and his elder brothers, gratifying the queen's hatred; portions pulled down for a Baal-temple (cf. 2 Kings 11:18); 'bestowed on Baalim' = 'made into the Baals' (Hosea 2:8; 8:4).

debates.question: Who are 'the sons of Athaliah' that broke up the temple?

sides.position: Her sons by another marriage, not Ahaziah's line
Ahaziah and his brethren, the royal princes, at the queen's instigation

schools.summary: Gill defers to the fuller account of the chest in 2 Kings 12.
Clarke points to the parallel notes on 2 Kings 12:9.

Ellicott contrasts the impersonal chronicler ('the king said, and they made') with the more original Kings ('Jehoiada took a chest and bored a hole in its lid') and locates the chest in the court, just inside the gate.
Henry admires the novel expedient: a second method when the first failed; the novelty itself drew cheerful giving — an invention to please men's humour may bring them to their duty.
Gill: the proclamation was made by heralds through Judah and Jerusalem.

Ellicott glosses 'uttered a voice in Judah' (cf. Prov. 1:20), notes the verse is peculiar to the chronicler with his fondness for the people's willingness (1 Chron. 29:6), and corrects the versions' 'until it was filled' to 'until they had made an end' (2 Chron. 31:1).
Gill: hearing the proclamation and its easy method, the people found it agreeable and gave with ready hearts.
Henry dwells on the cheerful giving — a great deal thrown in with joy — and the lessons: a few active leaders carry a good work, and a means that pleases men's humour may bring them to their duty.

themes: the high point of the reign

schools.summary: Gill locates 'the king's office' in a chamber of the temple where the officers met.

Ellicott details the emptying by the king's scribe and the high priest's officer, the Levites' part, and the chronicler's substitution of 'the high priest's officer' for Kings' 'the high priest' — done to guard the high priest's dignity in a later age when the monarchy was gone; 'day by day' = time after time.
Gill: the money was given to the overseers to pay the several artificers.

Ellicott reads 'the doer' collectively as the Levitical inspectors (cf. 2 Kings 12:11), 'hired' as a continuous action (1 Chron. 22:15), and notes the chronicler abridged the fuller account; Keil gathers the sense of the trades employed.
Henry: king, priest, and workmen all dealt faithfully — faithfulness the greatest praise of those entrusted with public treasure and business.

themes: the money paid to the workmen

schools.summary: Gill lists the trades — masons, carpenters, blacksmiths, brasiers — that finished the work.

Keil and Ellicott expound the metaphor 'a bandage was applied to the work' (a figure of healing, cf. Neh. 4:1; Jer. 8:22; 30:17) and 'set the house in his state' as restoration to its original measure (Exod. 30:32); the verse is peculiar to the chronicler.

themes: the summit of the good years

schools.summary: Gill: the vessels were made after the repairs were finished.
Wesley: new vessels were needed because Athaliah and her sons had carried off the old ones (v.7).

Keil catalogues the vessels of service and altar (Num. 4:12); Ellicott ('spoons' = kappoth, Exod. 25:29) harmonizes the apparent clash with 2 Kings 12:13-14 (Kings tells what was done during repairs, the chronicler accounts for the surplus after) and marks the ominous 'all the days of Jehoiada.'
Gill marks the rarity of so great an age.

Keil weighs the kingdom's debt to Jehoiada — saving Joash, preserving David's house, ending Joram's idolatry — honoured with royal burial; Ellicott renders 'satisfied with days' (1 Chron. 23:1; Gen. 25:8) and allows a possible textual error in the 130 years.
Henry: born in Solomon's day, six reigns; buried among the kings with the encomium 'done good in Israel' — yet the little religion Joash had was buried in his grave.
Wesley echoes the six reigns and the great judgment that the death of holy, useful men brings on a people.
Gill: a fitting honour to the preserver of king and kingdom, and the king's uncle by marriage.
Clarke: Jehoiada had in fact been king, governing in Joash's name; the royal burial proves the people's esteem; Wesley glosses 'Israel' as Judah, the faithful remnant that owned God.
Keil grounds the honour in the good he did toward God and the temple, and marks the coming reversal; Ellicott adds his long regency and royal kinship (2 Chron. 22:11).
Gill: the princes, secretly idolatrous, durst not act while Jehoiada lived; now they press their suit.
Ellicott: they bowed as asking a boon — the royal sanction of idolatry (v.18) — and the king hearkened, like Rehoboam to his young courtiers (2 Chron. 10:8).
Clarke (Targum): they adored and seduced him, and he received their idols; Wesley: the plea was liberty of the high places, a cover for idol-worship God had confined to one place.
Henry: bad counsellors flattered him as freed from a priest-ridden tutelage; those who incline to ungodly counsel never lack ungodly counsellors.

themes: liberty of the high places as a cover

schools.summary: Gill: they came no more to the temple, forsaking its worship.

Ellicott names the object ('the Asherim and the idols') and the wrath (Num. 1:53) that took form in the Syrian invasion, the nobles' sin involving the nation; Keil identifies the wrath (2 Chron. 29:8) with Hazael's invasion.
Wesley: those who lately repaired the temple now forsook it — so inconstant a thing is man.
Henry: the princes restored the groves they had felled, and the king joined them — the reformers turned idolaters.

themes: wrath kindled and the Syrian rod

schools.summary: Gill dwells on God's clemency in sending prophets to reprove, warn, and recall them before executing wrath.
Ellicott fixes 'yet' = 'and,' 'to them' = 'among them,' and 'testified against them' as solemn adjuration in God's name (cf. 2 Kings 17:13), the refusal being settled.
Henry: the prophets' office is to bring people back to God; God left not himself without witness, but the people were so wedded to their idols that few received the testimony.
Gill glosses the Spirit's coming as the spirit of prophecy (Targum).

Ellicott renders the Spirit 'clothed' him (1 Chron. 12:18), fixes 'the priest' as Jehoiada's epithet, pictures him on the inner-court steps, and parallels 'forsaken/forsaken' with 2 Chron. 15:2; 12:5.
Clarke (Targum): he saw them burning incense to an idol on the day of expiation and hindering the priests; Wesley pictures the people still assembled in the court as he stood and charged them.
Henry: he told them plainly but without provoking language, the precept broken and the penalty ('forsaken/forsaken,' Deut. 31:16-17) — the minister's work to expose sin and expound providence.

themes: 'ye have forsaken... he hath forsaken you'

schools.summary: Gill: they conspired and procured the king's order to take his life.

Clarke recoils at the ingratitude — blood of the prophet, son of his saviour; when a man falls from God the devil enters; Wesley: stoned without colour of law, the Jews' 'seven transgressions in one.'

Ellicott: stoning was the penalty of idolatry (Deut. 17:2-5; Lev. 20:2) turned against the reprover; his words branded treasonable (cf. Jeremiah, Jer. 32:1-5; Naboth, 1 Kings 21:8-13); Christ's 'Zacharias' (Matt. 23:35; Luke 11:51) refers to this murder.
Henry: a popular tumult, sacred person, place, and message profaned, a covenant king murdering one he was bound to protect.

themes: the law perverted against the prophet

schools.summary: Gill spells out the forgotten kindness — preservation, throne, and counsel — repaid with the son's blood.

Keil reads the dying cry as the pivot to judgment; Ellicott renders 'behold and avenge' (Gen. 9:5; Ps. 10:4), calling it the older dispensation's blood-for-blood, contrasted with Stephen (Acts 7:60), yet also a prophecy soon fulfilled.
Henry: not revenge but prophecy — the blood cries like Abel's, and Christ makes the persecutors answerable (Matt. 23:35; cf. Rev. 6:10); ingratitude the worst of names.
Wesley: the LORD will make inquisition for innocent blood; Clarke marks how swiftly the requiring came — Syrians and assassination within the year.

debates.question: Is Zechariah's dying 'require it' a cry for personal vengeance or a prophecy?

sides.position: The older dispensation's blood-for-blood justice, softer than Stephen's Christian prayer
Not revenge but a spirit of prophecy — the certainty that God would avenge

themes: 'the LORD look upon it, and require it'

schools.summary: Gill: at the end of the year after the murder — so soon was the prophecy fulfilled.

Keil dates it 'at the revolution of a year' and notes the chronicler selects what shows the punishment; Ellicott (cf. 2 Kings 12:17) sees a small detachment sent to Jerusalem, the princes of v.17 routed and cut off as the ringleaders, the spoil sent to Hazael.
Henry: a small Syrian force routed them because God had turned enemy and fought against them, the Syrians his instrument.
Wesley: God swiftly avenged the prophet's blood, the princes singled out as the first beginners of the apostasy.
Gill notes the Syrian force was but few.
Henry: a handful routed a great host because they had forsaken God, the Syrians his instruments (Isa. 10:6-7; Deut. 32:30).

Keil: the LORD gave the great host into few hands as judgment; Ellicott renders the unique phrase, supplies the bribe of temple and palace treasures (2 Kings 12:18), and notes 'executed judgment' as divine requital (Exod. 12:12), the whole told from a prophetic viewpoint.

themes: the temple treasures given as bribe

schools.summary: Gill: the Syrians withdrew with what spoil they could get.

Ellicott: 'great diseases' (a rare word for pains, kin to Jehoram's at 2 Chron. 21:19); the servants slew him on his bed (2 Kings 12:20; cf. 2 Sam. 4:5); the plural 'sons' is likely rhetorical (2 Chron. 28:16) or a slip for 'son,' the deed a judgment not necessarily a revenge; buried apart from the kings (cf. 2 Chron. 21:20).
Wesley: the plural implies Joash slew Zechariah's brothers too; the assassins perhaps avenged that blood, as God intended.
Henry: the king slew other sons of Jehoiada; those who drink the saints' blood have their own given them; denied the royal tombs, not written with the righteous (Ps. 69:28).

debates.question: Does 'the sons of Jehoiada' mean Joash killed more than Zechariah?

sides.position: Literal — he slew Zechariah's brothers too, and the assassins avenged them
A rhetorical plural, or a scribal slip for 'son' (Zechariah); the LXX and Vulgate read the singular

schools.summary: Gill notes the first assassin is called Jozachar in the parallel at Kings.

Ellicott works the variants (Jozachar/Zabad, Shomer/Shemer/Shimrith), holds the mothers' names added not substituted, and reads them as a mark of the chronicler's distinct source; he rejects Thenius's moralizing as 'fancy determined by prejudice.'
Henry finds a providential irony: the assassins' foreign mothers show the forbidden idolatrous marriages recoiling in the kings' own destruction.
Clarke: the two were aliens, likely chamber-servants, and warns of the folly of kings trusting foreigners with their persons.

debates.question: What is the significance of naming the assassins' foreign mothers?

sides.position: A charged detail — forbidden idolatrous marriages recoiling, and the peril of alien servants
No moral emblem, only a mark of the chronicler's distinct source; the moralizing reading is prejudice

schools.summary: Gill notes 'his sons' concerns their number and names.

Clarke reads the 'burdens' as the Syrian tribute (or the sums for the repairs) and identifies 'the story' as the lost midrash of Kings; Wesley takes the burdens as God's judgments by the Syrians and by disease.

Ellicott shows massa' may mean prophetic oracles ('the multitude of oracles upon him,' cf. Isa. 13:1; Hab. 1:1; the prophets of v.19) or tribute (2 Chron. 17:11), and names the source as the Midrash of the book of the kings.

debates.question: What are 'the burdens laid upon him'?

sides.position: The Syrian tribute (or the funds for the temple repairs)
The prophetic oracles/threatenings sent against him (massa'), or God's judgments generally
